title: Ethiopia and Tigray Trade Offensives as a New War Looms in the Horn, While Xi's Washington Visit Opens With a Trade Truce Extension and Pezeshkian Rebuffs Trump's Ultimatum at the UN
subhead: UN General Assembly week moves from talk into action: the US and China extend their trade truce as Xi begins a landmark state visit, Iran's president rejects Washington's ultimatum while Tehran sets a five-day Hormuz deadline, and fears grow of a renewed Ethiopia-Tigray war in the Horn of Africa.

sections.heading: Xi's State Visit to Washington Opens With a Trade Truce Extension and AI Rivalry at the Fore
sections.body:
China's President Xi Jinping arrived at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday for a state visit, the first time since 1962 that a US president has personally greeted a foreign leader on the tarmac. Trump staged a red carpet welcome with a B-1 bomber flyover, and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing have agreed to extend their trade truce until January, pushing back the previous 10 November expiry. Under the existing arrangement, Trump lowered tariff rates on some goods in exchange for Xi loosening restrictions on rare earth minerals.

The visit is framed around artificial intelligence and the broader superpower contest. The BBC reports that the US and China are vying for AI supremacy 'while seeking to keep it under human control.' Xi, in a statement carried by China's state news agency Xinhua, said the two countries 'should be partners rather than rivals.' Bessent said after meeting Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng that the two sides discussed whether a more substantive trade deal could eventually follow, but the longer-term commercial relationship remains unresolved.
sections.whyItMatters: A personal, ceremonial Trump-Xi meeting plus a truce extension lowers the temperature on the world's most consequential bilateral relationship — and the AI dimension signals that technology, not just tariffs, is now the central axis of US-China competition.

sections.heading: Iran's President Rebuffs Trump's Ultimatum as Tehran Sets a Five-Day Hormuz Deadline
sections.body:
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian used his UN General Assembly address to reject President Trump's threat to 'annihilate the Islamic Republic' if no peace deal is reached, telling the chamber Iran will 'never bow our head or bend the knee.' He held up photos of civilians he said were killed in US strikes — more than 175 people, two thirds of them children, according to Iranian authorities — on a school in Minab and a sports complex in Lamerd. The US has denied striking Lamerd and says it is still investigating Minab.

Al Jazeera's live coverage reports that Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei says Washington has been given a five-day deadline to meet Tehran's conditions for opening the Strait of Hormuz. Pezeshkian said Iran remains 'ready for dialogue, diplomacy and negotiations without accepting the language of force,' but insisted the US blockade of Iranian ports would have to end as part of any deal. Separately, the AFP reports an attack on a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz killed an Indian sailor; India's foreign ministry condemned the attack and called for unimpeded passage to be restored. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters an Iran deal would require prolonged effort and that military options remain available.
sections.whyItMatters: Tehran is coupling a defiant public posture with a concrete, time-bound demand on the world's most important oil chokepoint, keeping the risk of renewed escalation — and renewed disruption to global energy flows — squarely on the table even while both sides profess openness to talks.

sections.heading: Trump's Board of Peace Unveils a $2.45bn Gaza Reconstruction Plan
sections.body:
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, President Trump's Board of Peace announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn, spread across 66 programmes over six months and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal. The board acknowledged substantial donations are still needed: it said $18bn has been pledged but only $280m handed over so far, and it estimates full reconstruction will require roughly $71.4bn over the next decade.

Jared Kushner, a Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faces 'different delays on different things,' telling stakeholders 'the goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed.' US envoy Steve Witkoff said the group had made 'real progress,' noting that hostage returns are complete and a ceasefire 'still exists.' The plan faces unresolved questions over security for those operating in Gaza, internal governance, and the disposal of unexploded ordnance and tunnel networks, as BBC reporting details.
sections.whyItMatters: The plan puts concrete numbers on Washington's post-war ambition in Gaza but the gap between pledges and delivered funds exposes how far reconstruction remains from reality — a reminder that the economic endgame lags well behind the diplomatic framing.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Tigray Accuse Each Other of Launching Offensives, Raising Fears of a New War
sections.body:
Ethiopia's government and the party controlling the northern region of Tigray have each accused the other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict. Getachew Reda, an adviser to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched operations in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced into a 'defensive war' following reported drone strikes.

The African Union's mediator for the 2020-22 war estimated some 600,000 people died as the conflict drove the region to the brink of famine. On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front announced an alliance with six other armed groups to remove the government in Addis Ababa. Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray after local forces reportedly took over Mekelle's airport. AU Commission chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf called for immediate de-escalation, while the US ambassador condemned the TPLF for launching 'a large-scale offensive' in what he called 'an unwinnable fight.'
sections.whyItMatters: A renewed Ethiopia-Tigray war would destabilise the Horn of Africa — a region already central to Red Sea security — and reopen one of this century's deadliest conflicts, with the airport seizures signalling a serious breakdown of the 2022 peace deal.

sections.heading: Turkiye and Iraq Agree to a Gradual Handover of the Bashiqa Base
sections.body:
Turkiye and Iraq have agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara's military base at Bashiqa, northeast of Mosul, to Baghdad, according to a statement from the Iraqi prime minister's office. The announcement followed a meeting at the UN between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, in which both pledged deeper security cooperation.

Al Jazeera reports the two sides agreed on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of 'outlawed foreign armed elements' — an apparent reference to the PKK in the mountainous Sinjar region — and agreed to expand bilateral trade, including the Development Road project. The Bashiqa base, established in 2015 to train forces fighting ISIL and hosting up to 600 Turkish soldiers, has long been a flashpoint that Baghdad viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
sections.whyItMatters: Handing the base back removes a persistent source of friction between Ankara and Baghdad at a moment of shifting Iraqi alignments, and signals Turkiye's willingness to formalise its security role in northern Iraq rather than impose it by presence.

bottomLine: UN General Assembly week produced substance rather than just rhetoric: the US and China extended their trade truce as Xi's state visit opened, Iran's president rejected Trump's ultimatum while Tehran set a five-day Hormuz deadline, Washington put a concrete figure on Gaza reconstruction, and a fresh Ethiopia-Tigray escalation raised the spectre of war in the Horn. The pattern is of simultaneous de-escalation — on trade, on ceremony — and unresolved, time-boxed pressure on the flashpoints of energy and the Red Sea. Watch the five-day Hormuz clock and the US-China trade talks for the next substantive moves.
